content: The findings presented are intended to serve as a foundation for further discussion and review. They are based on the conclusions of the State of Knowledge Review on Biodiversity and Health, Connecting Global Priorities: Biodiversity and Health and discussions held during a series of regional capacity-building workshops on biodiversity and health. These workshops, conducted jointly by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) between 2012 and 2018, involved representatives from health ministries, biodiversity conservation ministries across approximately 90 countries, indigenous community representatives, and invited experts. The findings are also informed by indicators designed to build resilience in socioecological production landscapes and seascapes, as well as other evidence-based tools that have been field-tested by various stakeholders. These tools are detailed further in the Further Resources section of the chapter. Guidance on mainstreaming biodiversity into nutrition and health policies and actions has the potential to indirectly transform health services. This transformation would shift the focus from a curative model with escalating costs to a model emphasizing diet-related disease prevention, resilience, and sustainability. This approach aligns with broader health system strengthening and universal health coverage goals, in collaboration with other partners. The identified indicators fall into three main categories: 1. Nutrition and health indicators. 2. Ecological resilience indicators. 3. Socioeconomic indicators. The indicators are designed for prospective use, serving as a basis for developing coordinated policies and action plans that integrate biodiversity, nutrition, and health. Their application is expected to contribute to the development of a harmonized framework, bridging methods and tools from research conducted in diverse settings. Field testing of these indicators is divided into three phases: Phase 1: Preparation and Stakeholder Identification This phase involves planning and organizing in-country consultations that bring together local, national, and, where applicable, regional and global stakeholders. The scope of the assessment is discussed with a broad group of stakeholders and tailored to reflect national and local capacities and circumstances. This phase also defines the assessment areas, compiles preliminary information about the landscape/seascape and resident communities, and identifies local stakeholders. A preliminary stakeholder mapping exercise is conducted to identify participants for the next phase. Phase 2: Field Testing – In-Country Workshops/Stakeholder Meetings During this phase, the assessment of the initial set of indicators is conducted in the country where the pilot testing occurs. The workshop typically includes an introduction to the guidance document and indicators, followed by discussions among participants. Stakeholders score each indicator based on existing measures, identify available data sources, highlight data and resource gaps, and prioritize entry points for intervention. Active and meaningful participation of a wide range of stakeholders is essential for assessing baseline status and identifying intervention points. Phase 3: Follow-Up The follow-up phase varies depending on the intended outcomes of the assessment. Generally, it aims to create an enabling environment for developing policies and actions that support healthy and sustainable diets while enhancing resilience in the country or community where the field testing is conducted. Broader aims may include: Strengthening adaptation, building social and ecological resilience, and promoting intergenerational equity through sustainable food systems. Reducing the high costs and inefficiencies of single-sector interventions and addressing the financial and social burdens of diet-related non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and poor health outcomes. Improving assessment, monitoring, and response to ecosystem changes and their impacts on diet-related health outcomes. Achieving greater policy coherence across governance sectors, including ecosystem, environmental, and public health management, to promote environmentally sustainable development in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and other relevant commitments. Field studies can contribute to tailored recommendations for cross-sectoral policy instruments, improving the sustainability of diets and food systems. Initial field testing may also identify opportunities for replicating and scaling up the indicators in other communities or regions. Monitoring and Reporting Progress Regular monitoring of progress in developing and implementing indicators can significantly promote human health and ensure that populations most dependent on biodiversity for food and nutrition are more resilient to global change. It is also crucial to ensure that biodiversity conservation and climate change measures (both mitigation and adaptation) incorporate health considerations. Progress in implementing this guidance can be monitored using integrated measures and indicators tailored to country capacities and circumstances. These measures can utilize existing data, complemented by household surveys and stakeholder consultations. Developing, field testing, and monitoring integrated indicators are critical steps in creating and evaluating relevant action plans and reporting instruments, such as National Climate Change and Health Action Plans (NCCHAPs), National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (NBSAPs), and other national reporting processes. If field testing occurs in Small Island Developing States (SIDS), alignment with the SIDS Accelerated Modalities of Action (SAMOA) Pathway should also be considered. For more detailed examples of how this guidance applies to SIDS contexts, refer to the WHO document on Mainstreaming Biodiversity for Nutrition and Health published in this series.
